sections.sectionSubTitle: Role: Senior Product Designer · Core team

text.text:
✨ Case summary

CoCounsel is Thomson Reuters' generative AI assistant for law and accounting professionals: people who have trusted Checkpoint, the industry's authoritative tax and law database, for decades.

Shortly after launch, I joined the Core Team to design the interaction architecture of the central Conversations experience: 8 projects to create a scalable interaction system that could make people trust this product.

👨‍🚀 My contribution

  • Led all 8 projects end to end - driving the full UX lifecycle from initial problem definition and user research to interaction architecture, UI mockups, and high-fidelity prototypes.

  • Worked closely with PMs, Content Designers, Accessibility Experts, Design Researchers, Design Managers, and Software Engineers - in order to articulate our goals and clearly define the project scopes.

  • Designed Product Requirement Documents and Roadmaps with scalable stages of each new feature, in order to act fast and consistently, to improve the experience of the whole product.

  • Helped different teams to maintain consistency and quality standards among their projects, by defining the base interaction systems for the Core Features from the product and expanding our Design System & A11y standards.

✏️ Key actions — Some topics to chat about

  • Product definition & strategy - designed the PRDs that became the product roadmap: Problem statements, Goals, User Stories, Feature Priorities, Benchmarks, Potential Success Metrics.

  • Research operations - Weekly usability sessions with practicing tax professionals, planned along with the Design Research team and working together on the implementation from the obtained insights.

  • Systems design - Design each project as a scalable framework, instead of a one-off solution, so the team can easily build on the top of the Core Design Language as CoCounsel evolves, keeping interactions consistent across the product.

  • GenAI interaction patterns - a five-phase visible thinking process, category-based citations, source backtracking, and data tables where every cell links to its evidence.

  • Cross-functional collaboration - from benchmark-informed decisions with product and engineering, to a welcome-email series built with Marketing in the product's design language.

🏆 Goals

  • The Source Backtracking raised engagement - answers where users interact with citations grew from 8% to 41%, tracked weekly by leadership and sustained after the launch weeks. Click-throughs to sources rose 27%.

  • Six operationally defined success metrics.

  • Built for what comes next - Provided one unified system to build on, which cut the time spent designing custom features and keeps the interaction logic consistent as the product grows.

Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel

"CoCounsel Tax & Audit" answers tax and accounting questions and backs every answer with citations from Thomson Reuters' Internal Database (The "Checkpoint" library) and primary sources like the IRS, FASB, GASB, AICPA, and IFRS.

Since launching in March 2025 it's been picked up by firms of all sizes across the US, saving people about 32% of the time on a task, according to the latest TR reports.

It is part of the wider CoCounsel platform, which reached one million users across 107 countries in February 2026, and it won a 2026 Stevie Award.

Lawyers and Tax professionals can not rely on a AI generated answer that they can not verify; and many users are senior practitioners with around twenty years of experience using Thomson Reuter's most popular product: "Checkpoint", which its still built around "Structured database research" interactions, and will now facing an open chat box.

Also, 3 constraints shaped every decision:

  • GenAI mechanics - probabilistic outputs, multi-minute processing on complex queries, failure modes that arrive unannounced.

  • Regulatory volatility - U.S. tax law was being restructured faster than official sources could publish, so live web data had to come in without eroding Checkpoint's authority.

  • Speed - the product had just launched and the strategy was fast implementation; every pattern had to be quickly shippable and widely reusable.

So we focused on making every answer verifiable at each step where a professional could ask, "why should I trust this?"

As a Senior Product Designer on the Core team, I was responsible for the definition of some of the base features for the Conversations experience con CoCounsel (A chat-based Gen AI platform), aiming to create a consisten system for the Core Design Language.

I led each of the 8 features below, working along with my design team and partnering with engineering, product, and research teams:

  • Document Upload

  • Error Handling framework

  • Tool Rendering (the "thinking" view)

  • Spreadsheets / State Charts

  • Citations and the Source Backtracking process

  • Web Search

  • Onboarding Chats

  • Welcome Emails

This also led me to define part of the Product Strategy and the Design Research related to them.

The main strategy was to work on the seven features as one architecture, not a backlog, with three main goals in mind:

  • Grounding: Being clear about that the AI knows

  • Verification: show its work and its sources

  • Adoption: lower the entry barrier for skeptical experts

title.text: 01: Being clear about that the AI knows

sections.sectionTitle: 01: Being clear about that the AI knows

text.text:
📁 Document Upload

In the high-pressure environment of tax accounting, the document ingestion experience was originally a fragmented "black box."

The team identified that users were struggling with "truncated identifiers" (not being able to tell which file was which) and a general lack of status feedback. This created a mental model mismatch: professionals didn't know if their local files had successfully reached the platform's knowledge base or if they were even referencing the right version of a document. For an expert whose work depends on accuracy, this uncertainty was a major barrier to trust.

🗃️ Document Upload

In the high-pressure environment of tax accounting, the document ingestion experience was originally a fragmented "black box."

The team identified that users were struggling with "truncated identifiers" (not being able to tell which file was which) and a general lack of status feedback. This created a mental model mismatch: professionals didn't know if their local files had successfully reached the platform's knowledge base or if they were even referencing the right version of a document. For an expert whose work depends on accuracy, this uncertainty was a major barrier to trust.

Watch the PRD example

content.text:
This was based on a diagnosis of the entire user experience to identify specific friction zones. I then used these findings to develop a comprehensive PRD that served as the project's strategic backbone, ensuring our roadmap was grounded in real-world professional needs.

Instead of treating features in isolation, we tackled the “Document Management” journey as a coherent, scalable system: Every phase of the document lifecycle (Selection, Upload, Error Handling, Processing and Reference) had its own distinct visual state and clear affordances, prioritizing clarity and professional trust throughout.

Before building the GUI, the team defined the roadmap through a comprehensive PRD to ensure alignment on these core pillars:

➡️ Problem Statements Identified:

  • Context Opacity: Truncated filenames and lost document origin (source/type) prevent experts from verifying data grounding.

  • Persistence Ambiguity: Uncertainty regarding the temporal scope; how and for how long a file influences the AI across turns.

  • Interaction Inconsistency: Fragmented silos between legacy menus and new drag-and-drop triggers cause cognitive friction.

  • Command Confusion: A gap between industry-standard "@" shorthand expectations and the existing UI response.

➡️ Strategic Goals:

  • Standardize Visual Feedback: Replace legacy elements with Design System components to ensure visual and functional consistency across all upload states.

  • Integrate Keyboard-First Interaction & Visual Grounding: Use industry-standard @ and / syntax with "Reference Chips" and autocomplete to provide a high-precision method for anchoring the AI to specific data sources.

  • Establish Contextual Hierarchy & Temporal Scope: Use markers and badges to differentiate between "General Knowledge" and "@Mentioned" files while clearly communicating the document's lifespan (Answer Vs Whole Conversation).

  • Deploy Actionable Error Transparency: Replace generic alerts with granular, per-file feedback (e.g., size or format issues) and integrated "one-click" retry functionality for immediate resolution.

➡️ Categories for User Stories:

  • Accuracy & Trust: Focuses on eliminating professional liability by ensuring full visibility of file names and ingestion status, preventing users from basing critical advice on failed or incorrect data.

  • Efficiency & Speed: Prioritizes reducing the "Time-to-Insight" through high-precision shorthand like @-mentions, allowing power users to bypass menus and anchor the AI to sources instantly.

  • Reliability & Consistency: Centers on building user confidence through predictable UI patterns (like standardized drag-and-drop) and clear visual signals that confirm the AI is actively "reading" the provided context.

➡️ Feature Priorities:

  • P0 (Safety & Reliability): Non-truncated identifiers (full names/icons), granular upload status, and one-click retry functionality.

  • P1 (Productivity): Standardized Design System ingestion across all flows.

  • P2 (Enhancements): Support for action commands (e.g., /summarize) directly within the chatbox.

➡️ Success Metrics:

  • Reliability: Error Resolution Rate (retries vs. abandons), Context Verification Speed (the time to identify a specific file within a batch of 10+ similarly named documents) and User Confidence Scores.

  • Efficiency: Shorthand (@) Adoption Rate and Time-to-Insight (TTI—from upload start to first grounded response).

➡️ Benchmarking Industry Standards:

  • We analyzed file-handling limits and referencing patterns across Gemini, Claude (Project context), ChatGPT (Connected apps), Microsoft Copilot (M365 integration), Perplexity (Spaces), Grok (Cloud connectors), and Notion AI (Referencing connectors).

We translated those strategic goals into a Component-Based Interaction System. We wanted the UI to feel "state-aware" so the user always knew exactly what the system was doing.

➡️ The Smart File Chip

We redesigned the basic file attachment into a multi-functional "Smart Chip."

  • Visual Badging: We integrated file-type icons (PDF, Excel, Word) so users could identify their files at a glance.

  • Hover Dynamics: To fix the "Truncated Name" issue, we added a hover interaction that reveals the full file path and name, which is critical for precision during audits.

➡️ Deterministic States

We established a visual language to manage expectations during LLM processing

  • Uploading: A gray background with an active loader to signal progress.

  • Error: A red background with a warning icon—moving away from cryptic code errors to actionable states.

  • Ready/Mention: A distinct design for files already in the knowledge base vs. those just uploaded.

  • Shorthand Reference (@ Mentions): We designed a "Search-as-you-type" menu triggered by the "@" key. This allows power users to pull in existing documents without ever taking their hands off the keyboard.

  • Unambiguous Drop Zones: We built high-contrast "Drop" areas that provide clear visual confirmation of the target zone, ensuring a reliable drag-and-drop experience.

➡️ Reliability & Trust

By replacing generic errors with "Actionable Error Chips," we intended to improve the Error Resolution Rate, giving users the clarity to retry or fix issues themselves.

➡️ Contextual Certainty

The combination of badges and hover states eliminated guesswork, allowing users to verify their data context significantly faster during high-volume sessions.

➡️ Operational Efficiency

The focus on TTI as our primary benchmark ensured that the tool remained a professional-grade asset rather than a source of latency.

➡️ Professional Fluidity

The "@" mention system successfully bridged the gap between "local files" and "system knowledge," making the chat feel like a unified, professional-grade workstation.

title.text: 02: Showing the AI's work and every source behind it

sections.sectionTitle: 02: Showing the AI's work and every source behind it

text.text:
🧭 Cited Sources Panel

For tax professionals, a "correct" answer from an AI is useless if it cannot be verified against official sources.

Standard AI citation patterns (typically small numerical footnotes) are insufficient for high-stakes audits because they lack context regarding the nature or reliability of the source.

The challenge was to design a system that allowed experts to navigate dozens of sources of varying authority (official legislation vs. web news vs. internal files) without being overwhelmed by information density.
Extended details

content.text:
We moved beyond generic footnotes to create a Semantic Citation System.

This system explicitly categorizes evidence into distinct categories, allowing users to prioritize official Thomson Reuters "Checkpoint" data over external web sources or local documents. The interaction focuses on a seamless loop between the AI’s summary and the original evidence.

➡️ From Footnotes to "Citation Chips"

We redesigned static numbers into interactive "Chips." These chips provide immediate semantic context by displaying the source category (e.g., "Checkpoint", "Web" and "Documents") and the quantity of sources supporting that specific claim. Clicking a chip serves as a direct trigger to open the auditing panel.

➡️ The "Cited Sources" Lateral Panel

I re-designed a dedicated sidebar with tabbed categorization (All, Checkpoint, Web, Documents). This structure prevents "list fatigue" and allows users to filter for the specific type of evidence they need for their audit.

➡️ Integrated Document Viewer

To minimize context switching, the "Cited Sources" panel was designed to transform into a high-fidelity document viewer. When possible (Checkpoint or local files), users can read the original text directly within the panel; for external web links, the system provides structured cards with direct browser deep-links.

➡️ Elimination of "Hallucination Anxiety"

By providing a clear, categorizable path to the source of every claim, we directly addressed an important barrier to AI adoption in the tax industry: the fear of non-verifiable information.

➡️ Enhanced Auditing Speed

The semantic chips and tabbed sidebar allow professionals to perform "spot checks" or "deep dives" with significantly lower cognitive load compared to traditional unstructured citation lists.

➡️ Systemic Scalability

The "Citation Chip" and "Source Card" patterns were built as reusable components for the core UI Kit, ensuring that any future tool added to the CoCounsel platform (like the "Charts" or "Filters") inherits the same high standard of transparency.

💭 "Thinking" process

High-stakes queries often require several minutes of LLM processing, and the industry-standard "loading spinner" fails the "Visibility of System Status" heuristic. This lack of transparency causes "black-box anxiety," where users are unable to verify if the system is grounding its research in correct sources or hallucinating its logic path. For a professional with legal liability, this opacity is a critical risk factor.
Extended details

content.text:
I designed an Interaction System based on "Narrative Transparency," transforming internal system logs into a human-readable research trajectory. This approach was heavily influenced by observing background processing patterns in relevant AI products like Gemini and Copilot, but I tailored it to meet auditing standards required for tax and legal professionals.

The objective was to externalize the LLM’s "Chain of Thought" into a structured, audit-ready UI that moves away from "AI magic" toward "AI reasoning." By benchmarking how industry leaders handle high-latency transparency, I developed a framework that provides enough detail for verification without overwhelming the user. We categorized this research lifecycle into five semantic phases to ensure the narrative felt logical and trustworthy:

1️⃣ Starting the Search: We show the user that the AI has understood their question and is preparing the right "tools" to find the answer.

2️⃣ Checking the Expert Library: The system explicitly shows it is looking through the "Checkpoint" database, TR's gold-standard library for tax and law.

3️⃣ Reviewing Your Documents: If the user uploaded files, the AI confirms it is reading them to make sure the answer is tailored to their specific case.

4️⃣ Looking for Live Updates: The AI checks the live web to see if there are any brand-new law changes or news that aren't in the official books yet.

5️⃣ Writing the Final Answer: Once the research is done, the AI tells the user it's now putting everything together into the final response or chart.

➡️ Progressive Disclosure

To keep the UI clean, I built a collapsible "Logic Tree." Users see a simple summary of what's happening at first. If they want to audit the AI's work, they can click to expand any step and see exactly which links or files are being used.

➡️ The "Stop Switch" (User Agency)

Research showed that most participants would stop a query if they detected the AI going down the wrong path. I implemented a persistent "Stop" button active during the thinking phase, allowing for early intervention and saving both time and system credits.

➡️ Building a Reusable UI Kit

I expanded our ShadCN library to include standardized AI state components. I defined "Active," "Done," and "Error" states to ensure consistency across the entire v1 platform.

➡️ Keeping the UI "Alive" (Dynamic Feedback)

To handle unpredictable latency, I designed the micro-copy to update dynamically (e.g., "Scanning page 5..."). This reassures users who are multitasking that the system hasn't frozen.

➡️ Persistence of Information

Addressing a specific usability find where expanded sections would auto-collapse on new updates, I implemented a "persistent expansion" logic so users don't lose their place while auditing a live process.

Based on our research process and feedback from tax professionals, we established several key goals to ensure the "Tool Rendering" added real value to the daily workflow:

➡️ Effortless Visibility

Explore showing high-level process steps automatically. Participants wanted to see the workflow without needing to click, reducing the interaction cost for a quick status check.

➡️ Confidence & Predictability

Implement explicit progress indicators (like a progress bar or estimated time). Users multitask while the AI "works," so they need clear expectations to manage their time effectively.

➡️ Deep-Dive Navigability

Make internal references (like specific sections of "Reviewing Checkpoint") clickable. For complex tax codes, users don't just want to know that we checked a source; they want to jump directly into the source to verify the logic.

➡️ Guidance on Scrutiny

Investigate "Confidence Scores" or accuracy indicators. Tax experts want to know when they need to apply extra scrutiny to an answer versus when the AI is operating on high-certainty data.

➡️ The "Audit Trail" Requirement

Even if users don't check the process every time, the mere presence of the "steps" builds trust. It serves as a psychological safety net—an audit trail they can rely on for client-facing advice.

🔢 Structured answers

For tax accountants and auditors, raw text is an inefficient format for comparing complex data across multiple dimensions, such as varying tax rates across 50 states over several years. The primary challenge was to take unstructured GenAI responses and organize them into a structured, high-density format that allowed for rapid auditing and cross-referencing without losing the context of the underlying citations.
Extended details

content.text:
To maintain consistency and scalability, I moved away from designing a static table and instead designed a modular interaction system for the table cell. Each cell was treated as a self-contained information architecture (IA) unit containing:

1️⃣ Primary Answer: The core data point.

2️⃣ Clarifying Metadata: Secondary text for nuance.

3️⃣ Audit Trail: Direct links to "Primary Law" and "Editorial Analysis" sources.

➡️ The Artifact Side Panel

To solve the horizontal space constraints of a chat window, we implemented an "Artifact" pattern where clicking a chart result opens a side panel covering 2/3 of the screen. This provides the necessary "breathing room" for complex multi-column tables.

➡️ Minimalist Visual Hierarchy

I performed a "clutter audit" of the initial MVP, stripping away redundant borders and visual patterns. This ensures that when 50+ cells are visible at once, the user’s focus remains on the data rather than the UI noise.

➡️ Responsive Logic & Constraints

I defined a rigorous system for column behavior across 1080p and 720p resolutions, including min/max cell lengths. This ensured that regardless of the query complexity (e.g., comparing 3 vs. 10 states), the information remained legible.

➡️ MVP Utility

Recognizing the user's need for external reporting, we prioritized a "Export to CSV" feature, allowing professionals to move their verified data from CoCounsel into their existing Excel workflows.

➡️ Accelerated Decision Making

By enabling "at-a-glance" comparisons across states and years, we drastically reduced the time accountants spent manually collating information from multiple chat turns.

➡️ Enhanced Auditability

The inclusion of source-specific links within every cell built a direct bridge between the AI's summary and the "Checkpoint" source of truth, satisfying the rigorous verification standards of tax experts.

➡️ Workflow Continuity

The CSV export and side-panel interactions allowed the tool to fit seamlessly into the professional's broader work ecosystem, rather than being an isolated chat experience.

🌐 Web Search

Tax professionals operate in a high-volatility environment where legislation can change overnight. While Thomson Reuters’ "Checkpoint" database is the industry gold standard for official records, there is often a critical time lag between a news announcement and its official publication. Users needed CoCounsel to bridge this gap by consulting mainstream media and external sources without compromising the tool's perceived authority

media.caption: Mockup example: Web Search trigger on +Menu redesign

text.text: Extended details

content.text:
The goal was to make external web data feel as structured and verifiable as internal database records. My strategy focused on:

1️⃣ Contextual Awareness: Integrating "Websites consulted" directly into the "Thinking Process" (Project 1) so users could see the live search happening.

2️⃣ Visual Hierarchy: Designing a distinct "Web Source" visual language (using the "Globe" icon and specific metadata) to immediately differentiate external news from official internal citations.

3️⃣ User Agency & Control: Implementing a toggle within the "+" menu settings. This allows users to strictly limit the AI to official "Checkpoint" data when legal certainty is paramount, or enable Web Search for real-time agility.

➡️ The "+" Menu Integration

I redesigned the interaction flow in the global command menu to include the Web Search toggle. This placement ensures that source control is always "top of mind" before starting a query.

➡️ Modular "Web Source" Card and Citation Chip Design

I designed a modular card component for external results that ensures visual consistency whether it appears in the chat stream or the dedicated sidebar. These cards include a Website Title, URL, and Timestamp—the latter being a critical audit feature that allows tax experts to verify if the news is the most recent update available.

➡️ Systemic Filtering

I extended the "Cited Sources Panel" to include a specific "Web Search" tab. This categorization allows "Power Users" to audit external vs. internal sources separately, reducing the cognitive load required to verify a complex answer.

➡️ Real-Time Agility

Enabled CoCounsel to be useful for "breaking news" tax scenarios, significantly expanding the product's use cases beyond historical research.

➡️ Trust Through Differentiation

By clearly labeling external sources, we maintained the integrity of the "Checkpoint" brand while still providing the broader information users requested.

➡️ Cross-Project Integration

These patterns were not isolated; I integrated the Web Search visual language and logic into the "Tool Rendering" (Thinking Process) project, the "Citations" framework, and the "Cited Sources Panel." This ensured that every project mentioned in the platform's ecosystem shares a unified method for handling non-proprietary data.

title.text: 03: lower the entry barrier for skeptical experts

sections.sectionTitle: 03: lower the entry barrier for skeptical experts

text.text:
💬 Onboarding Chats

A significant segment of CoCounsel users are senior tax and legal professionals who have relied on traditional, static databases like "Checkpoint" for decades. Transitioning to a Generative AI chat interface presents a steep learning curve; these users often face "blank canvas paralysis," unsure of how to structure a prompt or what specific capabilities the tool offers.

media.caption: Mockup example: "Create an Email" onboarding chat

text.text: Extended details

content.text:
To bridge the gap between traditional search and conversational AI, I designed an onboarding system that utilizes affordances and familiar UI patterns.

Rather than a forced tutorial, I integrated "Example Chats" directly into the existing Chat History sidebar. This approach allowed users to "peek" into high-quality interactions without the pressure of formulating their own first query.

➡️ Contextual Simulation

I curated three "Golden Path" examples that highlighted core platform value:

  • Email Drafting: Transforming complex data into a professional client email.

  • Analysis: Reviewing and extracting insights from locally uploaded documents.

  • Research: Handling general accounting queries against the proprietary knowledge base.

➡️ Familiar Sidebar Integration

I placed these samples in a dedicated "Example Chats" category within the sidebar. By leveraging the affordance (where users already expect to find and click on conversations) we ensured the entry point felt natural. Using the same list-item pattern as real chat history allowed users to intuitively understand that these were clickable, interactive records they could explore.

➡️ Setting the Standard for Prompts

Each example contained a pre-filled query and a complete AI-generated response. This served as a silent "tutorial" on the ideal tone, structure, and length of prompts required to get professional-grade results.

➡️ Accelerated User Activation

By providing immediate "Proof of Value," we reduced the cognitive load required for the first interaction, helping non-tech-savvy users move from "spectators" to "active users."

➡️ Mental Model Alignment

The examples established clear expectations for AI behavior, reducing frustration and "trial and error" by demonstrating exactly what the tool can (and cannot) do.

➡️ Systemic Consistency

By leveraging the existing "Chat History" architecture and adding custom sorting/filtering rules, we ensured the onboarding experience felt like an organic part of the platform's evolution rather than a bolted-on feature.

text.text:
✉️ Welcome Emails

In a B2B environment, a firm’s purchase of a software subscription does not automatically guarantee user adoption. Many professionals continue to use legacy workflows, either unaware of the new tool's capabilities or hesitant to change their habits. The challenge was to create a "re-engagement" loop that transformed passive subscribers into active CoCounsel users.
Extended details

content.text:
I collaborated with the Marketing and Graphics departments to design a 5-part email lifecycle series.

The strategy focused on incremental value delivery: starting with basic access and moving toward complex, high-value tasks. I ensured the transition from "Inbox to App" felt seamless and low-friction, focusing on the continuity of the experience.

➡️ Curated Value Pillars

The team defined the feature highlights for the core emails in the sequence:

  • Email 1 (The Kickoff): Focused on reducing entry barriers (Sign-in tutorial) and the core promise of "Citations for Trust."

  • Email 4 (Document Intelligence): Introduced the "Document Upload" and "Summarization" workflows to solve specific data-heavy pain points.

  • Email 5 (Efficiency Mastery): Highlighted "Prompt Templates" to help users move beyond basic chat.

➡️ Visual Continuity

Since this project originated outside the core UX department, a gap analysis was performed between Thomson Reuters' marketing guidelines and the CoCounsel UI. We synchronized banners, typography, and button styles to ensure the emails looked and felt like the platform itself.

➡️ The Unified CTA

Every email centered around a single, high-intent action: "Ask your first question." This direct deep-link minimized "choice paralysis" and funneled users directly into the chat interface.

➡️ Intended Product Utilization

By proactively addressing common friction points (like sign-in and source verification) in the inbox, the team aimed to drive higher activation rates for firms that had already invested in the subscription, ensuring the tool's value was visible early in the user lifecycle.

➡️ Cross-Departmental Synergy

The team successfully bridged the gap between marketing communication and product experience, ensuring a consistent brand voice across the entire user journey.

➡️ Multi-Modal Learning

By integrating links to short-training videos within the emails, the team provided a "safety net" for users who preferred visual learning over text-based prompts, catering to diverse professional learning styles.

text.text:
✨ Case summary

👨‍🚀 My contribution

As a Product Designer on the Assistive Experiences team from the Microsoft 365 Studio, my main focus was to define the interaction design systems for conversational AI incubation on M365 products, which involved: 

  • Define and articulate the scope of different features in collaboration with PMs, Design Managers and Devs. 

  • Led internal research to learn about the hypothesis and results from other teams from the M365 Core Studio (such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook & Microsoft 365 Chat), in order to deal with the ambiguity and abstract ideas that the incubation processes required.

  • Facilitate the experimentation process by designing sketches, conversational interactions, user stories, user flows, mockups and rapid prototypes that aimed to make the most out of new Semantic Machines, LLMs & Generative AI technology for new interactions systems. 

  • Propose roadmaps with scalable stages of each new feature (Crawl - Walk - Run).

✏️ Key actions — Some topics to chat about

  • Collaborate with the Design Research team

  • User's Journey Maps

  • Testing Semantic Machines modules

  • Defined Design Concepts along with PMs, Devs and Design manager

  • Workshops

  • Roadmap documentation

  • Sketches, Wireframes and Mockups

  • Graphic User Interface

  • Conversational User Interface

  • Voice User Interface

🏆 Goals

In order to “productize” this technology, the M365 Design Studio needed to consider how conversational experiences could be implemented into existing products, such as Outlook and Teams, so we developed an interaction model that augments the main UI of each feature by layering a “Cortana” module on top of them.

media.caption: Brief example of how Cortana behaves on Outlook

text.text:
Cortana on M365 mobile apps

Since the acquisition of Semantic Machines Inc in 2018, Microsoft has been investing in Natural Language, LLMs and Generative AI technology to improve the productivity metrics among Microsoft 365 Users. This led to the incubation of several features that were being experimented within Cortana's integration to M365 products, such as Outlook and Teams.
These features later became part of the construction of "Microsoft 365 Copilot" productive capabilities, which evolved into "Microsoft 365 Chat" a bit later.

As a Product Designer on the M365 team, I focused on the exploration of different Conversational AI capabilities, proposing new ideas and defining frameworks for new features, such as:


Search
The tool should be able to identify user’s request and answer accordingly, acknowledging that they could be expecting an email, a file, a calendar event, or even a specific piece of information inside any of these.

Search Refinement
People should be able to correct or add variables to the search process without having to start over again.

Keyword Spotting
“Hey, Cortana!”

Semantic Machines Productivity Assistant testing
QA testing, bug reports, documentation to request metrics for our long term strategy.

Commanding
The assistant should be able to help people navigate the app and change the desired settings by asking it with natural language.

And some others, just like:

  • Onboarding for First Time Users

  • Frequently Asked Questions

  • AI Assistance for frontline workers

High fidelity prototyping

This prototype is meant to show that:

  • The feature can be enabled by voice

  • The command will show a change on the color theme from Outlook’s inbox

  • Cortana’s success feedback will include interesting phrases and an emoji matching the selected theme

  • Quick-acess touch buttons invite you to continue interacting with the feature

  • Cortana’s response should change even if you choose the same colors every now and then

  • It works with special/limited-time themes

  • You’re able to access the settings menu through it

3 Steps Roadmap

This plan was based on the input data that we were able to get from people searching on their Outlook's app. One of the main focus was to make people aware how to take better advantage of the Natural Language capabilities so we could move on with more complex interactions, such as writing a whole email or edit a whole bunch of items.

Phase 1 - Voice input directly on the current search bar

A quick win: Create a "String" to start a query at the search bar, using the user's voice input.

Phase 1 - A generic fallback

A fence that can also communicate that we can't accomplish the request - for now.

We also offer a glimpse of what the current Cortana's capabilities are.

Phase 2 - Refinement

We keep the same solution, about placing the voice input on the current search bar, but we offer one more step to narrow their search.

This is also meant to tell the users that they can ask for specific results by stating this variables through natural language the next time they talk to Corana.

Phase 3 - Complete consistency using voice interactions

The assistant can be present on the complete search process, by using the emerging tab, while mantaining the Natural Language interactions, to mantain consistency with the whole system.

There's also a "Direct answer" module, in which Cortana selects a single email that matches with all the variables that the users send and stating which ones are being prioritized to refine the search to that point.

After selecting the suggested email, Cortana will offer you possible next steps that you can access to with Natural Language, such as writing a Reply, Forward the email or Play it with voice.

🤖 Copilot for Microsoft 365

Microsoft and OpenAI began their partnership in 2019, this collaboration has since grown with significant investments and joint efforts to advance AI technology. That allowed our team to articulate new capabilities into our Natural Language conversational system, such as LLMs with Generative AI, to improve the productivity metrics among Microsoft 365 users.

This led to the incubation of several features that are currently being tested & refined, to be implemented through Copilot Agents which I’m not allowed to showcase just yet. However, I'm happy to chat about every geeky topic referenced on these set of brief articles, about the future of the Generative AI being applied to productivity tools.

caseStudies.name: How to implement Gen AI into a Design Process: The error-handling framework for CoCounsel Tax & Audit
caseStudies.subtitle: Role: Senior Product Designer · Core team

title.text: How to implement Gen AI into a Design Process:

subtitle.text: The error-handling framework for CoCounsel Tax & Audit

sections.sectionSubTitle: The error-handling framework for CoCounsel Tax & Audit
sections.sectionTitle: How to implement Gen AI into a Design Process:

text.text:
✨ Case summary

I designed the error-handling framework for the Conversations experience. It's also the project where I worked out a deliberate way to use Gen AI in my own design process: creating a defined framework and leaning on it for the pattern recognition capabilities to fill out on the gaps and accelerate the expected outcomes.

In a complex Generative AI ecosystem, errors are inevitable—ranging from LLM timeouts and "hallucination" crashes to local network drops. The challenge was to move away from generic "Something went wrong" messages and build a systemic framework that manages user expectations, preserves work-in-progress, and maintains thread integrity.

👨‍🚀 My contribution

  • Led the Core Interaction Design for the Error Handling framework for the platform; one consistent system for every kind of failure, instead of one-off error states scattered across features.

  • I worked closely with engineering, product, content design, and accessibility to make each error state correct, clear, and usable.

  • I defined and shared a reliable way of bringing AI into the design process, being deliberate about what to hand the model and what to keep as a real design decision, which the team was able to pick up to define their own work.

✏️ Key actions — Some topics to chat about

  • Interaction Design for AI failure and uncertainty

  • Decision frameworks

  • Benchmarking other AI products

  • Collaborative design (Designed Collaborative board with Devs, PMs and Designers)

  • User Journeys and User Flows

  • Sketches, Wireframes and Mockups

  • Content Design for error messages

  • Contribution to the internal UI Kit (ShadCN AI-state components)

  • Implementation of Accessibility (A11y) standards

🏆 Goals

Across this project, the work added up to a few things for both the people using the product and the team building it:

  • Kept professional trust intact: Clear, proactive guidance on how to fix an error turned moments of frustration into clarity, so a failure didn't push people to abandon the tool mid-task.

  • Saved people's work: Preserving drafts and file selections meant a technical hiccup didn't cost someone their progress.

  • Built for what comes next: Provided one unified system to build on, which cut the time spent designing custom failure states and keeps the interaction logic consistent as the product grows.

  • The way of working spread, too: The deliberate approach to using Gen AI here (what to hand the model, what to keep as a real design decision, etc) became shared good practices that keeps helping other designers define their own processes.

Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel

"CoCounsel Tax & Audit" answers tax and accounting questions and backs every answer with citations from Thomson Reuters' Internal Database (The "Checkpoint" library) and primary sources like the IRS, FASB, GASB, AICPA, and IFRS.

Since launching in March 2025 it's been picked up by firms of all sizes across the US, saving people about 32% of the time on a task, according to the latest TR reports.

It is part of the wider CoCounsel platform, which reached one million users across 107 countries in February 2026, and it won a 2026 Stevie Award.

The main challenge around this projects were about the fact that the product was new and scaling fast. Also that the people using it are tax and legal professionals who are personally on the hook for the advice they give; for them, an AI that "might be wrong", or that they can't double-check, isn't a shortcut, but a severe risk.

That left me with two problems to solve at once: every interaction had to protect trust, and the team needed one shared design language so that standard held as we added features.

As a Senior Product Designer on the Core team, I was responsible for the definition of some of the base features for the Conversations experience con CoCounsel (A chat-based Gen AI platform), aiming to create a consisten system for the Core Design Language.

I led each of the eight features below, working along with my design team and partnering with engineering, product, and research teams:

  • Document Upload

  • Error Handling framework

  • Tool Rendering (the "thinking" view)

  • Spreadsheets / State Charts

  • Citations and the Source Backtracking process

  • Web Search

  • Onboarding Chats

  • Welcome Emails

This also led me to define part of the Product Strategy and the Design Research related to them.

media.caption:
Using AI to design AI
(and keeping the wheel)

text.text:
🤝 Maintained Professional Trust

By providing clear, proactive explanations of how to solve an error, the team transformed moments of frustration into moments of clarity, preventing users from abandoning the tool during high-stakes tasks.

❤️‍🩹 Maximized Work Recovery

The focus on "State Preservation" (saving drafts and file selections) directly improved the platform's perceived reliability, ensuring that technical hiccups don't result in lost professional billable hours.

📈 Systemic Coherence for Future Growth

The team now possess a coherent, unified system to build upon, significantly reducing the time spent on custom failure states. This framework allows for the seamless integration of new error types and warnings as CoCounsel evolves, ensuring consistent interaction logic across different features and sections of the product.

📝 The way of working spread, too

The approach I took to bringing Gen AI into this project — being deliberate about what to hand to the model and what to keep as an actual design decision, then checking and adapting its output by hand — became a shared set of good practices for the team.

That strategy for putting AI into our workflows is helping other designers refine their own processes, so what came out of this project is useful well beyond error handling itself.

Context

In a complex Generative AI ecosystem, errors are inevitable, ranging from LLM timeouts and "hallucination" crashes to local network drops. The challenge was to move away from generic "Something went wrong" messages and build a systemic framework that manages user expectations, preserves work-in-progress, and maintains thread integrity.

The Strategy

I started this project by designing a general framework that could help me understand and communicate the current error & fallbacks logic for the platform. After collecting every possible error (prioritizing the ones that were triggered most in the last months), I categorized them into 3 distinct buckets, each with its own set of interaction rules and GUI Patterns:

  1. AI Response Failures: Handling incomplete or failed generations.

  2. Input Validation Errors: Correcting user-side issues (e.g., empty prompts, oversized files).

  3. Network & Service Errors: Managing connectivity drops and session expirations.

Setting the rules for the Gen AI Tool to fill in the gaps

Acknowledging that this tool couldn't be taking the actual design decisions, I defined which were the parts that I was actually expecting it to fill and then guided it to it by:

  1. Defining the context and the objective

  2. Selecting the sources (local and public) from where it should take the raw info from

  3. Providing the general framework of interaction systems that would be impacted by each decision

  4. Providing a general process (3 questions to be asked) to follow to define the missing info from each Error State

    1. Technical Capability: Is the system technically capable of supporting this specific interaction right now under this error condition?

    2. Mental Model & Trust: Would allowing this interaction mislead the user about the state of the conversation, the system's performance, or the status of their last prompt?

    3. Friction vs. Protection: Would blocking this interaction create unnecessary friction that doesn't protect the user from anything real, or does it protect them from performing an action doomed to fail?

  5. Providing mandatory constraints

  6. Setting a brief example of the expected output format

title.text: A collaborative effort to refine the results

sections.sectionTitle: A collaborative effort to refine the results

text.text:
Manual intervention & the Collaborative Board

The information gathered from the Gen AI's answer was manually checked and structured into a Figma's collaborative board, so I could make sure that the logic behind each case case was consistent and wouldn't create confusion within the team.

Also, because even if the whole system followed the rules with 100% accuracy, it was necessary to make exceptions on certain details to prioritize actual empathy and understanding of the user's context, for example: Disabling the "Send" button when necessary, but maintaining the chatbox active so people wouldn't lose their progress while creating prompts. This distinction was important because on some other cases the whole component, or even the whole tool, needed to be disabled to create a "hard stop" and avoid making the error or confusion even bigger.

And finally, in order to add my own comments based on the most relevant questions, opinions or interactions that the team previously had on different meetings (even from discussions related o other projects) around all the topics and systems that this new proposal touched; to truly make it adoptable and scalable for all the other projects, it needed to be fully adapted to the team's actual context.

media.caption: An example from the first case on the board

text.text:
Synthesis - Design requirements

After the team got into an agreement for the general rules and exceptions, I was able to set up the key solutions with the following requirements:

1️⃣ Thread integrity

When a response is unresolved, the thread disables every option to progress on the conversation, so you can't pile a new question on top of a broken one and leave a gap in the record.  There must be a clear distinction between "Unable to progress on the conversation" and disabling components that are related to it but serves other purposes, like the Text Box being a feature not just to send a message, but to design a prompt.

2️⃣ Keeping what’s useful; Remove possible bias

When a response cuts off but what came through is real and cited, I kept it on screen and labelled it as partial, instead of throwing it away.  On the other hand, block the whole answer on scenarios in which the interruption could generate a biased perception of the answer, for example, while generating charts or spreadsheets.

media.caption: Example cases for the first 2 requirements

text.text:
3️⃣ Honest lockouts

When the network or service is gone, we should lock the whole interface rather than half-unlock it.

An interface that flickers back to life and then fails again is more unsettling than just saying plainly that you're offline.

4️⃣ A way out, not a dead end

Every error needs a direct action: "Try again", "Sign in again", and where the system could recover on its own, it just tells you it's back.  When acknowledging the escalation of the issue, a Contact Support should option shows up.

media.caption: Example cases for the last 2 requirements

text.text:
Individual components

While going through the process to get this clarity, some aspects from the system could be worked along with the Content Design team and the Accessibility experts, so the results of this whole effort could be influenced by the best practices of each area.

media.caption: Selection of ShadCN's Design System components & Content Design for the main error messages

text.text:
Applying the Interaction System to the GUI

The final documentation included everything that was needed for the team to follow up on every decision that was taken. It was important to make this as easy to navigate as possible and to communicate the reasoning behind it all, so other teams in the future could continue building on the top of it.

The User Flows contained:

  • A Mockup for every step of the process.

  • An escalation process (In which the interface acknowledge that there was an error that needs to be solved).

  • Interaction notes (With accessibility and behavior details) for the disabled components

  • Notes with the reasoning behind specific steps, especially when there was an "exception to the system" held in there.

  • Variable scenarios, like the error happening at the beginning of the conversation VS on an ongoing conversation.

  • Placeholder notes for missing component states, being built by other teams.

media.caption: User Flow Sample: Network connectivity is lost mid-way through a file upload.
User Flow Sample: The AI begins streaming a text response but fails partway through, leaving incomplete text.
Documentation Sample: Error scenarios, categories, Required Components, Mockups, User Flows, Interaction Notes, etc.

title.text: Productivity AI-Powered Features for Microsoft Edge & Windows 11

sections.sectionTitle: Productivity AI-Powered Features for Microsoft Edge & Windows 11

media.caption: Some of the interventions that were proposed

text.text:
✨ Case summary

👨‍🚀 My contribution

As a Senior Product Designer on the Microsoft 365 Studio, my main focus was to: 

  • Work closely with PMs, Design Managers, and Devs from different neighbor Microsoft 365 product teams (from Teams, Outlook, Windows 11, To Do, Search and Edge) in order to articulate our goals and clearly define the features scopes to drive improvements in Microsoft Feed's discoverability and retention on the New Tab feature.

  • Led internal research to learn about the hypothesis and results from other teams at the M365 Core Studio (such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook & Microsoft 365 Chat), in order to navigate on deep ambiguity that the incubation processes required.

  • Facilitate the experimentation process by designing their main architecture, wireframes, user flows, mockups and prototypes for new interactions systems that expanded on our current A11y & Fluent standards, to keep the discussion going and refine our ideas.

  • Propose roadmaps with scalable stages of each new feature, since the MVP of them needed to be resourceful, in order to act fast, and consistent, to holistically improve the experience of the whole product.

  • Helped different teams to maintain consistency and quality standards among their projects by improving the Fluent UI design system library for productivity features on mobile and desktop.

✏️ Key actions — Some topics to chat about

  • Collaborate with the Design Research team

  • User's Journey Maps

  • Desktop, Android and iOS interface implementation

  • Defined Design Concepts along with PMs, Devs and Design manager

  • Workshops

  • Roadmap documentation

  • Sketches, Wireframes and Mockups

  • Generative AI implementation

  • Accessibility (A11y) standards

  • Fluent Design System: Usage + Contribution

🏆 Goals

Our main goal with the Work Feed on the New Tab from Edge for Business is to make people able to discover relevant information from their work in just a glimpse. They should be able to scan their teammates activity on different Microsoft 365 products, such as Outlook emails, Teams meetings or updates on the documents they're working on.

The browser for business with innovations in AI and productivity

Edge for Business was anounced on May 2023 during the Microsoft Build conference. It was created to benefit productivity and security while browsing on the internet, especially focusing on separating work and personal browsing for hybrid workers.

This focus gave the team the opportunity to focus on a narrow user niche with very specific needs, and articulate this product goals with the ones that had been explored on other projects, such as Work Feed, the transformation of the New Tab feature and Company News.

media.caption: Microsoft Edge for Business | The new, dedicated work experience for Edge

text.text:
The Workfeed

Microsoft Feed is a relatively new product that helps people to connect with their coworkers by letting them discover and learn about their interests, teams and projects they're working with. It shows you a mix of content and activity from everything related to the Microsoft 365 suite.

Its main features are:

  • Discover relevant updates and progress related to important collaborations

  • Discover and learn new insights about your colleagues and people in your network

  • Prepare for meetings or learn what happened in meetings you couldn’t attend

  • Discover useful content related to your company or topics you're interested in

Windows 11 Widgets

The widget panel on Windows 11 can provide quick access to information from different sources, such as the Weather app, Watchlist, Traffic or News.

There is an active effort to bring productivity apps from the Microsoft 365 ecosystem for the enterprise users, such as Industry News and Meeting Insights, along with other ones that has been already implemented, like Outlook Calendar, Outlook's Inbox, and To Do.

Escalating the product

My main contribution during my time at this team was related to improving the usage, discoverability and retention metrics by contributing on the process to develop different features, such as:

  • New Workfeed widgets

  • New Windows 11 productivity widgets

  • Personalization capabilities for Edge's "New Tab"

  • Industry News experience

  • Onboarding for First Time Users

  • Information Architecture for deep re-structure of the Work Feed

  • High Contrasts, Keyboard navigation & Screen Reader accessibility standards for our backlog features

  • Smart Components for the Fluent Design System Library for AI related interactions on desktop and mobile.

title.text: "Your Next Meeting" - Enterprise widget on "New Tab" and Windows 11

sections.sectionTitle: "Your Next Meeting" - Enterprise widget on "New Tab" and Windows 11

media.caption: Waffle Menu implementation on Edge's Work Feed

text.text:
"Your Next Meeting"
Enterprise widget on "New Tab" and Windows 11

This module is meant to leverage the information that M365 suite and AI can gather an process in order to provide significant insights about your next meeting, such as:

  • Meeting name

  • Timestamp

  • Duration

  • RSPV

  • Location

  • Members

  • Link to Teams

    • Chat

    • Join

    • Expand

  • Latest shared files, relevant for the meeting purpose

media.caption: How much relevant info can we get into this tiny space?

text.text:
Flexible to different contexts

The module's system for the notification should be able to display every possible variable for different kind of meetings in a feasable way, such as:

  • Just 1 person was invited

  • 2 to 5 people were invited

  • more than 5 people were invited

  • Short title

  • Long title

  • Physical location

  • Remote meeting

  • Microsoft Team's group available

  • Microsoft Team's group unavailable

  • Just 1 relevant file located

  • 2 relevant files located

  • More than 2 relevant files located

  • Next meeting

  • Relevant upcoming meetings

Industry News Widget

This module was originally designed for the right pane of the Work Feed, in order to provide relevant news related to each user's profession. It is also a key intervention for Microsoft's Business, since "News" is one of the main ways in which the product generates profits.

The card should display

  • At least 6 relevant news

  • Its title

  • Thumbnail

  • When was it published

  • Order them by relevance, according to the user's activity and the time that it was published

  • State that the links are from external sources

  • Link to the main News section

✨ This intervention was the first to be successfully shipped and, by the first month, it was already being used by at least 46 million people each month!

Feed cards for carousell interaction

A mockup for the "Feed" section of the "New Tab", it was one of the 17 variables that we were able to design. It is currently on production and expected to be shipped soon, as the Industry News began to generate tracktion among Edge's users.

Notification

As we progress on our main goal with the New Tab on Edge, we are learning from our first internal experiments and data from user's behavior in order to expand on this vision, by designing new ways to articulate the user flows from all the productivity features that we currently have on Windows 11, our AI capabilities and every Microsoft 365 product.

This led us to create a couple of modules to invite new people to join the experience, such as this notification which was launched on August 2024.

title.text: A modular system for e-commerce

subtitle.text: Role: Product & Interaction Design Team Lead

sections.sectionSubTitle: Role: Product & Interaction Design Team Lead
sections.sectionTitle: A modular system for e-commerce

text.text:
✨ Case summary

👨‍🚀 My contribution

  • Led the Product Team through the whole Design & Implementation process

  • Defined an interaction system for Yalo's Product Teams to build their e-commerce chatbots and webapps in a consistent and scalable way

  • Established a standardized process, based on Human-Centered Design methods and tools, so different Product Teams could set their expected delivery time for different projects with new customers.

  • Designed a system to gather user's behaviour data and iterate on Yalo's products based on it

✏️ Key actions — Some topics to chat about

  • Design Research

  • Work and negotiation with stakeholders

  • Defined an MVP along with PMs, Devs and Design manager

  • Workshops

  • Roadmap documentation

  • Sketches, Wireframes and Mockups

  • Graphic User Interface

  • Conversational User Interface

  • Interaction Design for the modules behaviour

  • Defined success metrics and data gathering metods

🏆 Goals

The MVP was shipped and well recieved by Pollo Campero's customers. After we studied our first success metrics, "Meta" prepared an article to highlight the project as a success case on "Facebook for Business" blog.

The modular system was well recieved by Yalo's Product Teams and it's currently being used by different grocery shopping, restaurant, and packed goods companies, such as:

  • Pollo Campero

  • Domino's Pizza

  • Bimbo

  • Aurrerá (Part of Walmart)

  • Panda Express

  • Nestle

media.caption: A prototype of our MVP for Pollo Campero's restaurant

text.text:
Yalo's mission

Yalo, partnered with Meta, provides automation and user behavioral data for LATAM industries to improve their CRM and the “WhatsApp for Business” product. The systems made for the "Consumer Packed Goods" and "Retail" categories often require e-commerce platforms for them to be adopted by their staff and customers.

Given the Yalo’s history and its growth as a startup, it was important for the Retail product to consider each of the slight variants that are required by the industry: Selling combos, adding items to an order, customize different dishes, different hierarchical levels to organize 50, 100, 500 or thousands of products, among others.
The main objective of this project was to automate customer service for Pollo Campero, but by thinking and designing it as a system, we were able to replicate our success for different customers.

title.text: Product & Interaction Design Team Lead

sections.sectionTitle: Product & Interaction Design Team Lead

text.text: As a Product Designer on the “Support & Improvements” area, I was responsible of providing solutions to our “Conversational UX Designers” for them to build the best possible interaction systems, mostly by taking the ownership of a chatbot project myself and prioritizing its consistency, scalability, analyze its metrics and documenting the results with “Best Practices” insights for the related industry, being retail, in this case.

Commerce Webapp
Designed a modular webapp system, using Atomic Design principles, that could be customized for different kinds of needs.

Automatize Frequently Asked Questions
Analyze the customer inputs to define the most requested info and train the Machine Learning module so it can identify when to provide it.

Conversational structures
Design different user flows with their respective fallbacks, considering the “Designing for resilience” methods, so people can refine their searchs instead of starting from scratch each time they commit a mistake, such as:

  • Order taking

  • Account sign up

  • Payments

  • Frequently Asked Questions

  • Recommended dishes and discounts

  • File a complaint

Feature improvements
Design a strategic roadmap based on the data analysis of different metric points being measured along the experience.

🤖 Bot personality
(Research + Definition)

This process was defined prior to this project. As we constantly needed to negotiate the need of a Design Research process on our first projects, this deliverable was designed to comunicate our stakeholders the value of understanding their clients to connect with them through a familiar interaction.

It sets the bases for the tone and type of responses that can be designed to adapt the conversation to the context through which the user is navigating without losing the consistency of the conversational design. It is usually based on brand manuals, social media strategy and all the info we can gather about the users of the tool.

By analyzing stakeholder expectations, worker processes, and user needs for WhatsApp meal ordering and customization, I identified patterns that were applicable to other design and product teams facing similar challenges, so I proposed a series of internal workshops so we could be able to connect the dots of the whole system, share findings, and advance towards the same goal.

media.caption: Quick drafts to define every required feature for the different stages of the user's Journey

text.text:
📐 Flowchart + Wireframe + Wireflow

Recognizing the unique strengths of the graphical interface compared to the current conversational interface, I designed the interaction to feel like one unified experience, preventing it from seeming like a workaround.

This document was also needed to negotiate the required time and resources with Yalo's and Pollo Campero's leads for our expected goal.

media.caption: First attempt to articulate Graphical and Conversational UI

text.text:
🛒 GUI design System for e-commerce

This modular web app system provides four base variations that can be tailored for different needs, with optional features for Product Teams to meet the unique requirements of each project.

Using Atomic Design principles, we achieve standardized quality for our web apps, significantly shorten the design cycle, and improve client negotiation outcomes.

This system is often used in e-commerce for grocery shopping, food delivery, restocking stores and more.

media.caption: Documentation for the first step of the Weabapp
Design documentation to communicate how the modules should behave with different inputs

text.text: First set of mockups so more team members with different perspectives could participate on Co-Creation workshops

The Beginning of a Successful Journey

The tool was shipped and well recieved by Pollo Campero’s customers. After measuring how the people were using it and refining some of the initial implementation points, Meta prepared an article to highlight it on their “Facebook for Business” blog, which was meant to promote the Whatsapp API.

This helped us to get green light to other e-commerce projects from the backlog, which we were able to accomplish thanks to the scalable strategy that was presented at the beginning of this one.

text.text:
Grocery App Modules:
A Quick Example

To better organize products and align with the familiar physical store shopping experience, it employs a six-level hierarchical structure. An example of this architecture is:

Level I - Groceries.

Level II - Dairy.

Level III - Lala (brand).

Level IV - Yoghurts.

Level V - Strawberry Yoghurt 250g (Product).

Level VI - Description of Strawberry Yoghurt.

text.text: Register, adding items through coversational interactions, item list on webapp, cart on webapp

media.caption: "How can a digital device that seeks to replicate reality be more comfortable?"

text.text:
Objective

Establishing standards that allow people to use and take advantage of this new technology in the most comfortable and seamless possible way.

Context

Virtualware is an international company specialized in projects involving software, hardware and Virtual Reality services. This project began as an exploration of the technological, physical and cultural environment of VR to detect needs, since the company had found an opportunity in the businesses involving this technology; however, the company had no design standards to resolve these projects; thus, we sought to lay the groundwork to improve the overall quality of all upcoming projects.

Problems

This project emerged under the context of a team that had been developing virtual reality projects without design requirements to meet technological needs from a people-centered perception.

  • How can we create a more enjoyable experience with a screen directly in front of our eyes?

  • What are the ideal design parameters for generating VR content?

  • How would people from different cultural backgrounds react to the content that has been created?

  • What is the value that can be created for them with such technology?

  • How can a new technology be linked to the users’ context?

Research

At the beginning of this project, we made an immersion in the context of people at different levels:

  • Social. To understand issues related to the demand for products and services in different contexts.

  • Cultural. With the purpose of knowing people's consumption preferences and the value of the purchased items and services in their everyday lives.

  • Technological. To learn about the level of technological immersion in various technologies, since, at that time, VR was an emerging technology.

  • Market. To be able to know the competition and the products related to VR from the perspective of people's consumption.

All of the above to detect opportunities and strengths regarding the company's VR projects.

The other starting point that we considered was an immersion in the parameters that companies such as Google and Samsung had established until then.

text.text:
Key Findings

  • Currently, the hardware required for VR has several limitations, such as battery life, and mobile devices’ specifications, which make them heat up and affect their performance.

  • People's consumption decisions tend to be based on the image they want to build around their identity, which is a determining factor in the type of content they share in social networks.

  • Having a screen in front of the eyes is often tiring for users, a problem that reduces the time viewers can use VR sets.

  • The use of applications tends to be based on the activities that people do, especially hobbies and work.

  • VR platforms require specific elements adapted to the people’s physiological needs.

  • The number of users interested in learning about new technologies is very large; people that are the least interested are those who hardly use digital technology and older people, with a greater sense of conventionalism.

  • Young people are more interested in traveling to real-life places such as Japan and Germany, rather than being able to "live" an experience in a fantasy world, such as the world of Harry Potter, Star Wars, etc.

  • One of people's hobbies is watching movies or series, not just on weekends, but also making time for them during weekdays.

  • The use of an immersive application with a VR set is not clear for many users; thus, it is necessary to optimize processes such as cardboard assembly, video selection and instructions.

text.text:
UI in virtual reality

Based on the research, we designed diagrams for virtual reality interfaces, with the recommended parameters in terms of distance, contrast, colors, fonts and element positioning in the environment.

media.caption: These findings came from the conclusions of the analysis of Samsung’s and Google’s parameters, from the conclusions we reached in the immersion in the context of people, usability tests and other approaches to VR experience and interaction.

text.text:
Reference mockups

The purpose was to communicate all this information to the GUI design team, concept artists and 3D modeling for the ideation sessions regarding the scenarios they would be designing.

These mockups reflected the requirements to achieve a longer time of usability of the VR headset, for example:

  • Menus 3 meters away

  • Airport scenery

  • Font that can be read at the lowest possible resolution (Open Sans)

  • Setting a greater contrast between colors in areas that require a focus of attention. Sound feedback. Biaural recording, where possible.

  • Interactivity at 180 degrees for seating experiences, 360 for standing and moving.

  • Defining standard heights based on the target audience each project.

  • Reducing glare during transitions.

Videogames and VR activations

In the end, the standards were applied to various videogames and educational experiences, highlighting those designed for promotion in fairs of the Mexican "Secretaría de Turismo" in Europe, such as:

Mayan Ball

The famous pre-Hispanic ball game. The purpose was to score points with the HTC Vive controls placed on the participants' hips. The control also contained banners with the points scored by each participant and the time remaining.

Monarca - Visita Michoacán

An experience on rails. The physical stage simulated the basket of a hot-air balloon; thus, when users put on the headset, they would land on a field with thousands of monarch butterflies.

Ferrocarriles mexicanos

Streaming platform concept

A major part of the project was the collaboration in the design of a streaming platform for virtual reality content. Its purpose was to obtain better information on the acceptance of a wider audience (beyond gamers) of these types of services.

It was presented with the restrictions that a real service would have, such as stories of no more than 3 minutes and reddish scenes to reduce the damage caused to the eyes by frequent blue light.

The team contributed with the understanding of potential users, especially their context, tastes and needs to generate strategies leading to the success of future projects aimed at the same audience.
